transcript.text:
Yes — we can narrow this down. Less commonly it is a belt, motor or drum-mechanical fault. 1. First look through the door when it should spin: is there water left in the drum? If there is, the likely issue is drainage rather than the spin motor.
2. If it was a single heavy item (bath mat, duvet, blanket) or a very small/overfull load, pause it, spread the items evenly or add a couple of ordinary towels, then try Spin again. 3. With the machine switched off and unplugged, turn the empty drum by hand. It should turn smoothly without scraping, grinding or feeling jammed. A stiff or noisy drum needs an engineer rather than forcing it. When it should spin, is there still water in the drum, and can you hear a pump humming or trying to drain?
no water left in drum, drained fine. it was just a big heavy rubber backed bath mat on its own, it sloshes bout then tries to speed up and gives up. came out dripping

That behaviour is very likely normal imbalance protection, not a failed spin motor. A single heavy rubber-backed bath mat holds water and sticks to one side of the drum; the slow sloshing/back-and-forth movement is the machine trying to redistribute it. If it cannot balance the load safely, it gives up the fast spin, so the mat comes out dripping. 1. Don’t spin the bath mat on its own. Check its care label too: many rubber-backed mats are not suitable for machine washing or spinning, as the backing can break up and damage the machine.
2. For a safe test, run a spin with a normal mixed, evenly spread load — a few ordinary towels/items is suitable. If it spins normally, there is no fault and no part is needed.
3. If you do wash a suitable mat again, add a couple of towels to help balance it, but avoid overloading. If it also repeatedly aborts spin with normal balanced loads, especially if it bangs hard or walks across the floor, then levelling or worn suspension would need looking at.
